summary: In 1895 Cuban nationalists rose again against Spanish rule, and Spain's harsh campaign against them, including the forced relocation of rural civilians into fortified towns, outraged opinion in the United States, whose newspapers covered the war intensely. When the battleship USS Maine blew up in Havana harbour in February 1898, intervention became likely. In April Congress demanded Spain's withdrawal from Cuba and the two countries went to war. On 1 May George Dewey's squadron destroyed the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay, and Filipino revolutionaries under Emilio Aguinaldo declared independence and besieged Manila. In Cuba, American troops took the heights above Santiago on 1 July, the US Navy destroyed Admiral Cervera's squadron on 3 July and Santiago surrendered on 17 July. US forces landed on Puerto Rico and took Guam, and the United States annexed Hawaii. An armistice on 12 August ended the fighting, and in the Treaty of Paris Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, making the United States a colonial power in the Caribbean and the Pacific.
casualties: About 2,450 US servicemen are estimated to have died, some 385 of them in combat and most of the rest from disease; Spanish deaths are estimated at about 15,000 to 16,000, the great majority from disease, while losses among Cuban and Filipino revolutionaries are not well recorded.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: The Spanish-American War, 1898

brief.hook: Cubans were fighting for freedom from Spain, Americans were outraged by Spain's harsh war, and when the USS Maine blew up in Havana, the United States went to war.

sides.who: The United States, fighting alongside Cuban rebels of the Liberation Army and Filipino revolutionaries under Emilio Aguinaldo
The Kingdom of Spain, with its garrisons in Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam

brief.resultLine: A ceasefire took effect on 12 August 1898, and in the Treaty of Paris of 10 December Spain gave up Cuba and handed Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States.

strategies.name: Dewey's strike at Manila Bay
strategies.text: Ready in Hong Kong before war began, Dewey's squadron steamed into Manila Bay and destroyed the Spanish fleet on 1 May. In one morning Spain lost its navy in Asia.

strategies.name: Blockade of Cuba
strategies.text: The US Navy blockaded Cuba from April and bottled Admiral Cervera's squadron up in Santiago. When it tried to break out on 3 July it was destroyed, and Santiago surrendered two weeks later.

strategies.name: Three years of Cuban rebellion
strategies.text: Cuban rebels had fought Spain since 1895, tying down a huge Spanish army. Disease and the guerrilla war had already worn it down before the first American soldier landed.

impact: The United States became a colonial power, ruling Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.
Cuba became independent in 1902, but under the Platt Amendment it lived as an American protectorate.
Filipinos who wanted independence fought their new American rulers in the Philippine–American War from 1899.
In Spain, the loss of the last great colonies set off a soul-searching known as the Generation of '98.

details: The battleship Maine had arrived at Havana on 25 January to protect American interests during the Cuban revolt. At 9:40 that night an explosion tore apart the front of the ship, killing about 260 of her 355 crew outright; a few more died later. A US naval court blamed an external mine, while a Spanish inquiry pointed to an internal coal fire. The cause is still debated, but 'Remember the Maine!' became a call for war.

On 11 April President William McKinley asked Congress for authority to end the fighting in Cuba. The joint resolution he signed on 20 April recognised Cuban independence, demanded that Spain withdraw and empowered the president to use the army and navy. Senator Henry Teller's amendment, passed by large majorities, disclaimed any intention to annex Cuba. An ultimatum was sent to Madrid, and Spain broke off diplomatic relations the next day.

Warships under William T. Sampson began blockading Cuban ports, and McKinley called for 125,000 volunteers. Spain declared war, and on 25 April Congress declared that a state of war had existed since 21 April. The blockade aimed to cut off the Spanish army in Cuba, more than 200,000 strong, and to force the Spanish navy to come out and fight.

Commodore George Dewey's Asiatic Squadron sailed from near Hong Kong and entered Manila Bay on the night of 30 April. At dawn on 1 May it attacked Admiral Patricio Montojo's ships anchored off Cavite and destroyed the whole squadron. Spain lost 77 killed and 271 wounded; US sources report no American combat deaths. Dewey held the bay and awaited troops, and the victory made the fate of the Philippines a question of the war.

Searching for the Spanish squadron of Admiral Pascual Cervera, which had sailed for the Caribbean, Sampson's ships bombarded the fortifications of San Juan on 12 May and found the harbour empty. The damage was limited, and the fleet soon left to look for Cervera elsewhere, but San Juan Bay was afterwards placed under blockade. Cervera instead reached Santiago de Cuba, where American warships soon blockaded him.

US warships arrived at Guantánamo Bay, east of Santiago, on 6 June to secure a sheltered harbour for the fleet. On 10 June the First Marine Battalion, about 650 men, landed and set up camp, and for three days Spanish troops attacked it. On 14 June Marines and Cuban insurgents, supported by the gunboat Dolphin, drove the Spanish from Cuzco Well, the only fresh water nearby. The bay was secured, and in 1903 the United States acquired it as a naval station.

Exiled to Hong Kong after an earlier revolt, Emilio Aguinaldo returned to Cavite with US Navy help on 19 May and took command of the revived revolution. By early June his forces controlled much of Luzon and were besieging Manila. On 12 June, at his family home in Kawit, he proclaimed the independence of the Philippines; 98 people signed the act. Neither Spain nor the United States recognised the declaration.

On its way to Manila with three troop transports, the cruiser USS Charleston under Captain Henry Glass entered Apra Harbor, Guam, on 20 June. The island's Spanish officials had received no news from Spain for two months and did not know that war had been declared. On 21 June Governor Juan Marina accepted an ultimatum and surrendered his garrison of 54 soldiers. Glass raised the American flag and sailed on to the Philippines the next day.

From 22 June William Shafter's Fifth Army Corps, including Theodore Roosevelt's volunteer cavalry, the Rough Riders, came ashore at Daiquirí and Siboney, east of Santiago de Cuba. The Spanish garrisons had withdrawn, and the landings were unopposed, while a Cuban advance guard skirmished with Spanish troops nearby. On 24 June American cavalry fought the first land battle of the war at Las Guasimas, after which the Spanish rearguard resumed its retreat towards Santiago.

On 1 July about 15,000 American troops attacked some 1,270 entrenched Spanish defenders on the heights east of Santiago. Henry Lawton's division took the village of El Caney after a day-long fight, while dismounted cavalry, including the Rough Riders and the Black soldiers of the 10th Cavalry, stormed Kettle Hill and infantry took San Juan Hill. The Americans lost more than 1,000 killed and wounded but gained the heights and laid siege to the city, aided by Cuban insurgents.

With American troops above the city, Admiral Cervera was ordered to break out. On the morning of 3 July his four armoured cruisers and two destroyers steamed out one by one and were chased down along the coast by the blockading fleet under Winfield Scott Schley, in the absence of Sampson. All six ships were wrecked or run aground. Spain lost 343 killed and some 1,600 to 1,900 captured, Cervera among them, against one American killed.

The Republic of Hawaii, whose leaders had overthrown the Hawaiian monarchy in 1893, sought annexation, and during the war Honolulu became a stopover for American troops bound for Manila, showing its value as a mid-Pacific base. Congress passed a joint resolution, the Newlands Resolution: the House voted 209 to 91 on 15 June and the Senate 42 to 21 on 6 July. McKinley signed it on 7 July, and sovereignty was formally transferred in Honolulu on 12 August.

Besieged on land and cut off from the sea after the loss of Cervera's squadron, the Spanish commander at Santiago agreed to surrender, and on 17 July the city was handed over to American forces. Disease, including typhoid and yellow fever, was spreading through Shafter's army, and from early August most of the invasion force was shipped home. On 26 July Spain asked for peace terms through Jules Cambon, the French ambassador in Washington.

General Nelson A. Miles chose the lightly defended south coast rather than the fortified east, and on 25 July his first 1,300 infantrymen came ashore at Guánica after a brief skirmish. Reinforced by further landings, American columns took Ponce, the island's second city, where the Spanish garrison withdrew, and began to advance inland along several routes towards San Juan, meeting little resistance in the south.

On 9 August American troops encircled the Spanish position at Coamo in central Puerto Rico and forced its defenders to retreat. Further along the road, at Asomante near Aibonito, Spanish and Puerto Rican troops held a mountain pass and checked the advance. Fighting stopped the next day on news of the armistice, before American forces reached San Juan. The campaign cost the Americans few casualties.

Cambon signed a protocol for Spain with the American government on 12 August, and hostilities were halted. Spain agreed to give up Cuba and to cede Puerto Rico and an island in the Marianas, while the fate of the Philippines was left to a peace conference in Paris. News of the armistice took time to reach distant fronts, and in the Philippines fighting went on for one more day.

Unaware of the armistice, the Spanish governor-general Fermín Jáudenes arranged with Dewey and General Wesley Merritt to surrender Manila to the Americans after a brief show of resistance, rather than to the Filipino revolutionaries who surrounded it. On 13 August American troops advanced and took the city, though real fighting broke out and men were killed on both sides. Filipino forces were kept out of Manila, and their resentment fed the coming Philippine–American War.

Signed in Paris on 10 December, the treaty ended the war. Spain gave up sovereignty over Cuba, which came under American military rule, and ceded Puerto Rico and Guam to the United States, along with the Philippines in return for $20 million. After a bitter debate over overseas empire, the US Senate ratified it on 6 February 1899 by 57 votes to 27, two days after fighting broke out between American and Filipino forces near Manila.
